$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following systems are homogeneous?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+t\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)\end{aligned}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

If $f≡0$ and $g≡0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-2, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=4, &  & d(t)=-1, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System II is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=1, &  & b(t)=2, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=t\end{aligned}
$$

- System III is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=0, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)+1\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)+6{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+{e}^{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t)+3t\end{aligned}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

If $f≡0$ and $g≡0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≢0$ and $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=3, &  & b(t)=2, &  & f(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t) \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=4, &  & g(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

- System II is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-1, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=5, &  & d(t)=6, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System III is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≢0$ and $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=4, &  & b(t)=0, &  & f(t)={e}^{2} \\ c(t)=0, &  & d(t)=1, &  & g(t)=3t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t).$ Which of the following vectors are solutions to this equation?

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 5t\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} \\ 2t-8\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we need to substitute each vector into the given matrix differential equation and check if it results in a true statement.

For ${x}_{1}(t)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t)^{′} \\ (5t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 5t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}2t \\ 5t\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, for ${x}_{2}(t)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{(2{t}^{2})}^{′} \\ {(2t-8)}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} \\ 2t-8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4t \\ 2\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}4{t}^{2} \\ 2t-8\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for ${x}_{3}(t)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{({e}^{2t})}^{′} \\ {({e}^{t})}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "${x}_{3}(t)$ only".

For ${x}_{1}(t)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{({e}^{-t})}^{′} \\ {(0)}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{(0)}^{′} \\ {({e}^{2t})}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(0)^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}+{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following systems of differential equations are linear?

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}^{2}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}(t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{2}(t))\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is not a first-order linear system of ODEs since it contains the terms $x_1^2(t)$ and $\sin(x_2(t)).$

- System II is a first-order linear system of ODEs since it can be written in the standard form, where

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=8t, &  & b(t)=-1, &  & f(t)=1, \\ c(t)=6, &  & d(t)=-2, &  & g(t)={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only the second system is linear.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t)=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)=0\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables). 
Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)
$$

where

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We have the following system.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t)=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ \sqrt{2} & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

If $f \equiv 0$ and $g \equiv 0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f \equiv 0$ and $g \equiv 0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-2, &  & b(t)=3, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=6, &  & d(t)=1, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System II is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f \not\equiv 0$ and $g \not\equiv 0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=1, &  & b(t)=0, &  & f(t)={t}^{3} \\ c(t)=0, &  & d(t)=-1, &  & g(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

- System III is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f \equiv 0$ and $g \equiv 0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=5, &  & b(t)=-1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-2, &  & d(t)=4, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only the first and third systems are homogeneous.

Here, we need to substitute each vector into the given matrix differential equation and check if it results in a true statement.

For $\mathbf{x}_1(t),$ we have

$$

$$

Now, for $\mathbf{x}_2(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{(t+5)}^{′} \\ {({t}^{2}-3)}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t+5 \\ {t}^{2}-3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t+5 \\ {t}^{2}-3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}5t+25 \\ -3{t}^{2}+9\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $\mathbf{x}_3(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{(5{e}^{t})}^{′} \\ {(-3{e}^{t})}^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}25{e}^{t} \\ 9{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ only."
